On RT-DETR-L, all seven evaluated LoRA-family configurations cross the predefined catastrophic threshold, supporting a calibrated Refuse-to-Full-SFT decision within the evaluated coverage. A controlled YOLO11 audit further shows that LoRA reduces peak training memory by 43.9 percent, although training takes 1.72 times longer. Within the evaluated detector families, placement policies, and calibration coverage, YOLO-PEFT replaces manual target-module trial and error with explicit, inspectable planning while preserving verified train-save-merge-export paths; refusal on unseen detector architectures remains an open validation problem. AI.motivation: Generic PEFT methods transferred from language models can fail silently on real-time detectors because heterogeneous operators and detection-specific components impose placement constraints absent from regular Transformer stacks. Manual target-module trial and error is the current practice, which is inefficient and error-prone.
AI.method: YOLO-PEFT formulates adapter placement as a constraint-planning problem. Given a detector graph, PEFT request, and resource budget, it assigns operator and semantic roles, evaluates explicit operator-validity, detector-semantic, graph-interface, and deployment predicates, records a reason code for each excluded module, and either emits a budgeted target-module plan or returns Refuse before training.

Refusal on unseen detector architectures remains an open validation problem.

title: KnifeHunter: Structured Local Representation Learning for Fine-Grained Knife Image Retrieval in Law Enforcement
summary: Knife-enabled violence presents a major public safety challenge, and law enforcement agencies require scalable tools for catalogue-level knife identification, intelligence analysis, and source attribution. Manual visual comparison is specialist, time-consuming, and difficult to scale under operational imaging conditions. We introduce KnifeHunter, an end-to-end forensic knife image retrieval system developed with UK law enforcement. The work contributes the KnifeHunter dataset, comprising 25,843 images across 543 knife classes from police evidence, retail catalogues, and border-force seizures, with structured metadata, Medium/Hard evaluation protocols, and large-scale distractor evaluation. We further propose CoRe-Net, a compact single-descriptor retrieval architecture that combines global context with spatially localised discriminative evidence. CoRe-Net introduces Structured Complementary Representation Learning (SCRL) to organise local evidence into complementary prototype-based representations, and Bi-Directional Reciprocal Fusion (BDRF) to integrate global and local evidence through residual projection and gated local-to-global injection. Using an EVA02-Base backbone and cosine-similarity retrieval, CoRe-Net achieves 88.0% mAP and 86.7% mP@10 on the Medium protocol, and 85.1% mAP and 83.8% mP@10 under distractor conditions. KnifeHunter was deployed by UK police forces during Operation Sceptre deployments from 2023 to 2025, achieving 99.2% mP@1 on field queries. These results demonstrate a practical and effective multimedia retrieval framework for fine-grained forensic knife matching in operational law-enforcement settings.

AI.tldr: KnifeHunter is an end-to-end forensic knife image retrieval system developed with UK law enforcement, introducing a new dataset of 25,843 images across 543 knife classes and a novel retrieval architecture (CoRe-Net) that achieves state-of-the-art performance on fine-grained knife matching, with successful deployment in real UK police operations.
AI.motivation: Knife-enabled violence is a major public safety challenge, and law enforcement needs scalable tools for catalogue-level knife identification and source attribution. Manual visual comparison by specialists is time-consuming, difficult to scale under operational imaging conditions, and limits intelligence analysis capabilities.
AI.method: The paper introduces KnifeHunter, an end-to-end retrieval system comprising: (1) a new dataset of 25,843 images across 543 knife classes from diverse sources (police evidence, retail catalogues, border seizures) with structured metadata and Medium/Hard evaluation protocols; and (2) CoRe-Net, a compact single-descriptor retrieval architecture using an EVA02-Base backbone that combines global context with spatially localised discriminative evidence via two key components: Structured Complementary Representation Learning (SCRL) for prototype-based local evidence organization and Bi-Directional Reciprocal Fusion (BDRF) for integrating global and local evidence through residual projection and gated local-to-global injection.
AI.result: CoRe-Net achieves 88.0% mAP and 86.7% mP@10 on the Medium protocol, and 85.1% mAP and 83.8% mP@10 under distractor conditions. The system was deployed by UK police forces during Operation Sceptre from 2023-2025, achieving 99.2% mP@1 on field queries.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a practical and effective multimedia retrieval framework for fine-grained forensic knife matching in operational law-enforcement settings, showing strong performance on both benchmark protocols and real-world field deployment.

title: Explanation Stability of Test-Time Adaptation in Computational Pathology: A Large-Scale Benchmark
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) has become a practical way to adapt deployed models to unlabeled target data, a setting that is especially relevant in computational pathology where staining, scanner, and cohort shifts are routine. While most TTA methods are evaluated by their effect on accuracy, clinical use also depends on whether the model's explanations remain reliable after adaptation. In this paper, we take a closer look at this largely unmeasured effect. We study explanation stability under TTA across two histopathology benchmarks, Camelyon17 and NCT CRC-HE, using five architectures ranging from convolutional networks to vision transformers and a pathology foundation model, seventeen TTA methods, and four attribution families. Across 2,958 adaptation runs, we observe a clear and systematic pattern: TTA methods differ sharply in how much they move model explanations, with frozen-backbone methods leaving attributions almost unchanged and continual methods such as CoTTA and RoTTA causing the largest drift. This effect is not uniform. Convolutional networks are substantially more sensitive than transformer and foundation-model backbones, and explanation drift increases with adaptation strength while remaining largely insensitive to batch size. Surprisingly, explanation stability is only weakly coupled to adaptation quality. Some methods preserve explanations almost perfectly while degrading calibration or accuracy, producing silent failures that would be missed by accuracy-only or explanation-only evaluation. These findings show that explanation stability is a distinct reliability axis for TTA in computational pathology. We release the metric, protocol, and full benchmark to support future work on adaptation methods that are not only accurate, but also stable and clinically auditable. Code: https://github.com/bahumanyarg11/tta-explanation-stability-pipeline

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates explanation stability under test-time adaptation (TTA) in computational pathology, finding that TTA methods vary widely in how much they shift model explanations—with frozen-backbone methods barely changing attributions and continual methods like CoTTA/RoTTA causing the largest drift. Crucially, explanation drift is only weakly coupled to adaptation quality, meaning some methods silently degrade calibration or accuracy while preserving explanations, revealing a distinct reliability axis that accuracy-only evaluation misses.
AI.motivation: While TTA methods are evaluated primarily by accuracy, clinical deployment in computational pathology also requires that model explanations remain reliable after adaptation (e.g., for auditing and trust). This largely unmeasured effect—explanation stability under TTA—needs systematic investigation.
AI.method: The study conducts 2,958 adaptation runs across two histopathology benchmarks (Camelyon17, NCT CRC-HE), five architectures (CNNs, vision transformers, pathology foundation model), seventeen TTA methods, and four attribution families, measuring how much model explanations drift during adaptation under various conditions (adaptation strength, batch size, backbone type).
AI.result: Frozen-backbone TTA methods leave explanations almost unchanged while continual methods (CoTTA, RoTTA) cause the largest explanation drift. CNNs are more sensitive than transformer/foundation backbones; drift increases with adaptation strength but is insensitive to batch size. Explanation stability is only weakly coupled to adaptation quality, revealing silent failures where methods preserve explanations yet degrade calibration or accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Explanation stability is a distinct and clinically relevant reliability axis for TTA in computational pathology, not captured by accuracy-only or explanation-only evaluation. The authors release their metric, protocol, and benchmark to support development of TTA methods that are simultaneously accurate, stable, and auditable.

title: RoRA: Role-Oriented Regional Allocation for Visual Token Pruning in MLLMs
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Code is available at https://github.com/LukieLuu/RoRA
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) encode images as long visual token sequences, making prefilling and KV-cache storage expensive. Existing training-free pruning methods select tokens by importance, diversity, or spatial coverage, but treat retained tokens as interchangeable and do not explicitly track which object-related regions are already covered. We present RoRA, a training-free framework that casts visual token pruning as role-oriented regional evidence allocation. Given a fixed budget, RoRA partitions tokens into a protected semantic core, complementary context, and fine-grained detail. It first calibrates text-conditioned attention with a positional prior and a prompt-calibrated object prior, then builds Attention-Anchored Regions (AARs) from high-confidence anchors as lightweight proxies for covered object support. Context is explored mainly outside AARs, while a small AAR-guided budget restores local detail; pairwise similarity is used only for context-stage redundancy filtering. Under matched budgets, RoRA consistently outperforms strong training-free baselines across LLaVA and Qwen-VL families, retaining most of the unpruned accuracy even at aggressive pruning ratios, e.g., 96.5% of full performance at 88.9% pruning on LLaVA-1.5, and improving over D2Pruner by about 5% on Qwen3-VL at 75-90% pruning. At a 66.7% pruning ratio, RoRA requires only 0.7 ms for token selection and reduces end-to-end inference time by 24.6%, corresponding to a 1.33x speedup over unpruned inference on an NVIDIA H800.

AI.tldr: RoRA is a training-free framework for visual token pruning in multimodal LLMs that casts token selection as role-oriented regional evidence allocation. It partitions tokens into a protected semantic core, complementary context, and fine-grained detail, using Attention-Anchored Regions (AARs) built from text-conditioned attention calibrated with positional and prompt-aware object priors. It consistently outperforms strong training-free baselines across LLaVA and Qwen-VL families, retaining 96.5% of full performance at 88.9% pruning on LLaVA-1.5, and achieves 1.33x end-to-end speedup on NVIDIA H800.
AI.motivation: MLLMs encode images as long visual token sequences, making prefilling and KV-cache storage expensive. Existing training-free pruning methods select tokens by importance, diversity, or spatial coverage, but treat retained tokens as interchangeable and fail to explicitly track which object-related regions are already covered, leading to redundant or insufficient visual evidence allocation.
AI.method: RoRA works in three parts: (1) calibrates text-conditioned attention with a positional prior and a prompt-calibrated object prior; (2) builds Attention-Anchored Regions (AARs) from high-confidence anchors as lightweight proxies for already-covered object support; (3) allocates a fixed budget across a protected semantic core, complementary context (explored mainly outside AARs), and AAR-guided fine-grained detail. Pairwise similarity is used only for context-stage redundancy filtering.
AI.result: Under matched budgets, RoRA consistently outperforms strong training-free baselines across LLaVA and Qwen-VL families. It retains 96.5% of full performance at 88.9% pruning on LLaVA-1.5 and improves over D2Pruner by about 5% on Qwen3-VL at 75-90% pruning. At 66.7% pruning, token selection takes only 0.7 ms, reducing end-to-end inference time by 24.6% (1.33x speedup) on an NVIDIA H800.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly modeling which object-related regions are already covered via role-oriented regional evidence allocation, RoRA provides an effective and efficient training-free visual token pruning strategy that preserves accuracy at aggressive pruning ratios while delivering meaningful inference speedups.

title: International Transfer of Stochastic Cortical Self-Reconstruction
summary: Stochastic cortical self-reconstruction (SCSR) enables personalized mapping of gray matter atrophy, a hallmark of neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), onto high-resolution cortical surfaces. Unlike conventional normative modeling approaches, which typically operate at a coarse regional level and remain inherently constrained by the covariates included during training, SCSR estimates an individualized healthy reference directly from the observed cortical thickness at the vertex level. This allows the detection of subtle, subject-specific deviations from healthy cortical shape. In this work, we investigate the generalization and transferability of SCSR, originally trained on UK Biobank (UKB) data, to an independent Chinese population dataset. Specifically, we evaluate the ability of SCSR-derived Z-scores to discriminate between healthy scans, individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and patients with AD, while also assessing model robustness across the lifespan. We compare four training strategies: direct application of the UKB-trained model, fine-tuning on Chinese data, training from scratch, and joint training on UKB and Chinese cohorts. As reconstruction backbones, we consider both a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a Spherical UNet (SUNet). Our results demonstrate that SCSR provides robust detection of cortical atrophy in the Chinese population across all evaluated models. The highest discriminative performance was achieved by the fine-tuned SUNet model (average pairwise AUC = 0.848), followed closely by the UKB-trained SUNet. Moreover, reconstruction errors remained low across the lifespan, even when the training population exhibited a substantially narrower age distribution, indicating strong cross-population transferability.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the generalization and transferability of Stochastic Cortical Self-Reconstruction (SCSR), a method for personalized mapping of gray matter atrophy, from a UK Biobank-trained model to an independent Chinese population. The study evaluates Z-score discriminative ability across healthy, MCI, and AD subjects using four training strategies and two reconstruction backbones (MLP and Spherical UNet). The fine-tuned SUNet achieved the best discriminative performance (average pairwise AUC = 0.848), with low reconstruction errors across the lifespan, demonstrating strong cross-population transferability.
AI.motivation: SCSR enables vertex-level, subject-specific detection of cortical atrophy without being constrained by coarse regional analysis or training covariates. However, its generalizability to independent populations beyond the UK Biobank training data remains unknown, motivating this cross-population validation study.
AI.method: The study compares four training strategies: direct application of the UKB-trained model, fine-tuning on Chinese data, training from scratch, and joint training on UKB and Chinese cohorts. Two reconstruction backbones are evaluated: a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a Spherical UNet (SUNet). SCSR-derived Z-scores are used to discriminate between healthy, MCI, and AD subjects, with robustness assessed across the lifespan.
AI.result: SCSR provides robust cortical atrophy detection in the Chinese population across all evaluated models. The fine-tuned SUNet achieved the highest discriminative performance (average pairwise AUC = 0.848), closely followed by the UKB-trained SUNet. Reconstruction errors remained low across the lifespan even with substantially narrower training age distributions.
AI.conclusion: SCSR demonstrates strong cross-population transferability from UK Biobank to an independent Chinese dataset, with fine-tuning providing marginal improvement. The approach holds promise for personalized, vertex-level cortical atrophy mapping in diverse populations and across the lifespan.

title: Geometry-Aware Camera Localization for Bronchoscopy
summary: Camera localization in bronchoscopy remains a challenging problem due to stringent accuracy requirements, real-time constraints, and limited training data. Compared to natural scenes, the confined anatomical structures demand millimeter-level precision, while intraoperative guidance necessitates low-latency inference. However, existing methods often fail to effectively exploit preoperative geometric priors, limiting their robustness and accuracy. To address these limitations, we propose a unified geometry-aware bronchoscope localization framework (GABL) that effectively fuses preoperative structural priors with paired intraoperative video to estimate 6-DoF camera poses. Specifically, to address visual ambiguity in complex airways, we propose a graph-guided coarse-to-fine localization scheme that effectively leverages structural priors for precise pose estimation. Furthermore, to mitigate pose jitter and bridge the visual-structural gap, we integrate a Transformer-based tracking model with a novel RGB-depth matching objective, jointly enforcing spatio-temporal and geometric consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method yields remarkable reductions of 8.37% and 31.76% in translation and rotation errors over the prior state-of-the-art, alongside 4 times inference speedup (33.6 FPS) for robust real-time bronchoscope localization. Project website: https://paulili08.github.io/GABL/.

AI.tldr: GABL is a unified geometry-aware bronchoscope localization framework that fuses preoperative structural priors with intraoperative video to estimate 6-DoF camera poses, achieving 8.37% and 31.76% reductions in translation and rotation errors over prior state-of-the-art with 4x inference speedup (33.6 FPS).
AI.motivation: Camera localization in bronchoscopy faces stringent accuracy (millimeter-level), real-time constraints, and limited training data. Existing methods fail to effectively exploit preoperative geometric priors, limiting robustness and accuracy.
AI.method: The framework (1) uses a graph-guided coarse-to-fine localization scheme leveraging structural priors to address visual ambiguity in complex airways, and (2) integrates a Transformer-based tracking model with a novel RGB-depth matching objective to jointly enforce spatio-temporal and geometric consistency, mitigating pose jitter and bridging the visual-structural gap.
AI.result: The method achieves 8.37% and 31.76% reductions in translation and rotation errors over prior state-of-the-art, with 4 times inference speedup (33.6 FPS) for real-time bronchoscope localization.
AI.conclusion: GABL demonstrates that effectively fusing preoperative geometric priors with intraoperative video enables more accurate, robust, and real-time bronchoscope localization.

title: Beyond Fluency: A Clinical Benchmark and Anomaly-Enhanced Baseline for Spine MRI Report Generation
comment: Maria Monzon and Catherine R. Jutzeler contributed equally as shared last authors. Accepted at the CV4Clinic Workshop, CVPR 2026
summary: Radiology reporting is time-consuming and subject to inter-rater variability, making automated report generation an attractive clinical application for Vision-Language Models (VLMs). We benchmark state-of-the-art VLMs on lumbar spine MRI with a focus on diagnostic accuracy and demonstrate that standard lexical and semantic metrics poorly reflect clinical correctness: fluent, well-structured reports can score highly while containing clinically meaningful diagnostic errors. To address this failure mode, we propose an architecture-agnostic framework that augments VLM inputs with spatially localized, disc-level anomaly heatmaps generated by a semi-supervised U-Net++ model. These heatmaps both improve anatomical sensitivity through explicit visual grounding and provide an independent interpretability output for clinical oversight, moving us closer to diagnostically reliable, visually grounded VLMs for lumbar spine MRI interpretation.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks VLMs on lumbar spine MRI report generation, showing that standard lexical/semantic metrics fail to reflect clinical correctness. The authors propose augmenting VLM inputs with disc-level anomaly heatmaps from a semi-supervised U-Net++ to improve diagnostic grounding and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Radiology reporting is time-consuming and subject to inter-rater variability, making automated generation valuable. However, existing VLMs can produce fluent but clinically incorrect reports, and current evaluation metrics do not capture diagnostic errors.
AI.method: Benchmark state-of-the-art VLMs on lumbar spine MRI; propose an architecture-agnostic framework that augments VLM inputs with spatially localized, disc-level anomaly heatmaps generated by a semi-supervised U-Net++ model to provide visual grounding and interpretability.
AI.result: Standard lexical and semantic metrics poorly reflect clinical correctness—fluent reports can score highly while containing clinically meaningful diagnostic errors. The heatmap augmentation improves anatomical sensitivity and provides independent interpretability output for clinical oversight.
AI.conclusion: Heatmap-augmented VLMs move closer to diagnostically reliable, visually grounded report generation for lumbar spine MRI interpretation.

title: Multiple Hypothesis Flow Estimation for Video Frame Interpolation under Matching Ambiguity
summary: Many flow-based video frame interpolation (VFI) methods synthesize an intermediate frame by estimating optical flow fields, warping the two input frames, and blending the warped observations. These latent flow fields are typically learned through image-level reconstruction supervision without direct flow annotations. In ambiguous regions containing repetitive or stochastic textures, rotating symmetric structures, or fast motion with blur, the matching evidence for a single query may contain multiple comparable and spatially separated peaks. Although the ground-truth intermediate frame provides indirect supervision, it may not uniquely identify the latent correspondence in ambiguous regions.When several locations provide multiple plausible matches, a single-flow estimator can retain only one displacement and discard the remaining candidates. If the selected match is incorrect or inconsistent with those of neighboring pixels, warping samples content from mismatched locations, producing ghosting, structural distortion, or blur.To address this limitation, we propose a multiple hypothesis flow estimation framework that preserves top-K candidate correspondences and selects one per location through a reliability-guided router. Each hypothesis is initialized from a coarse matching anchor and refined separately through anchor-centered local attention. Frame synthesis is thus conditioned on one selected flow-appearance hypothesis rather than a soft combination of candidate motions.Experiments on the proposed MA-HD benchmark and public VFI benchmarks show that our method achieves the best LPIPS and DISTS among the compared methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multiple hypothesis flow estimation framework for video frame interpolation that preserves top-K candidate correspondences in ambiguous regions (repetitive textures, symmetric structures, fast motion) and selects one per location via a reliability-guided router, improving perceptual quality metrics (LPIPS, DISTS) on public benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Single-flow video frame interpolation methods discard multiple plausible correspondences in ambiguous regions (repetitive/stochastic textures, rotating symmetric structures, fast motion with blur). When the selected match is incorrect, warping samples from mismatched locations causing ghosting, structural distortion, or blur.
AI.method: A multiple hypothesis flow estimation framework that: (1) preserves top-K candidate correspondences instead of a single displacement, (2) initializes each hypothesis from a coarse matching anchor, (3) refines each hypothesis separately through anchor-centered local attention, and (4) selects one hypothesis per location via a reliability-guided router. Frame synthesis is conditioned on one selected flow-appearance hypothesis rather than a soft combination of candidate motions.
AI.result: The method achieves the best LPIPS and DISTS scores among compared methods on the proposed MA-HD benchmark and public VFI benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Preserving and routing multiple flow hypotheses overcomes ambiguity limitations in single-flow VFI, enabling more perceptually accurate frame synthesis than soft combination or single-displacement approaches.

title: Human-AI Perceptual Alignment by Playing Hues and Cues
summary: Evaluating the perceptual alignment between Contrastive Vision-Language Models (CVLMs) and humans is typically constrained by traditional benchmarks that overlook fine-grained semantic and cultural nuances. In this work, we propose a novel evaluation framework that leverages the gamified, discrete color space of the board game Hues and Cues. By mapping the board's 480 color cells to the CIE xy chromaticity diagram, we calculate empirical perceptual distances across a carefully curated 100-word vocabulary spanning seven semantic categories. To properly contextualize model performance, we establish an empirical lower bound of expected error-the Human Consistency baseline-calculated via Leave-One-Out (LOO) cross-validation on a dense dataset of color associations collected from 325 human observers through a custom digital interface. We evaluate 162 models across multiple architectural families and pre-training datasets to assess their semantic color grounding. Our results demonstrate that while CVLMs successfully replicate human cognitive biases, such as idealized memory colors for concrete physical referents (e.g., food and plants), they systematically diverge from the human baseline in abstract, subjective, and pop-culture domains. We identify two distinct failure modes in severely misaligned concepts: semantic misclassification and a systematic uncertainty collapse into a default blue coordinate. Furthermore, we reveal that highly curated pre-training datasets are significantly more effective than massive, uncurated corpora in mitigating these severe misalignments. Ultimately, this work highlights that despite their broad categorization capabilities, current CVLMs still fail to capture the nuanced, localized consensus of human color memory, emphasizing the value of gamified tasks in exposing underlying model biases. The data and code are publicly available to test other metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel evaluation framework for Contrastive Vision-Language Models (CVLMs) using the color space of the board game Hues and Cues, mapping 480 color cells to the CIE xy chromaticity diagram and testing 162 models against a human consistency baseline built from 325 human observers. Results show CVLMs replicate human cognitive biases in concrete domains but diverge on abstract/pop-culture concepts, revealing two failure modes (semantic misclassification and uncertainty collapse into blue), with curated datasets outperforming massive uncurated corpora.
AI.motivation: Traditional benchmarks for evaluating CVLMs overlook fine-grained semantic and cultural nuances in perceptual alignment with humans. A gamified, discrete color space can expose subtle model biases and misalignments that standard evaluation methods miss.
AI.method: The framework maps the board game's 480 color cells to the CIE xy chromaticity diagram, uses a curated 100-word vocabulary across seven semantic categories, establishes a Human Consistency baseline via Leave-One-Out cross-validation on color associations from 325 human observers, and evaluates 162 models across various architectures and pre-training datasets.
AI.result: CVLMs successfully replicate human cognitive biases (e.g., idealized memory colors for concrete referents like food and plants) but systematically diverge from humans in abstract, subjective, and pop-culture domains. Two failure modes are identified: semantic misclassification and systematic uncertainty collapse into a default blue coordinate. Highly curated pre-training datasets mitigate severe misalignments more effectively than massive uncurated corpora.
AI.conclusion: Despite broad categorization capabilities, current CVLMs fail to capture nuanced, localized consensus of human color memory. Gamified tasks are valuable for exposing underlying model biases, and the released data/code enable further testing of other metrics.

title: InstanceSplat: Instance-Aware Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting for Scene Understanding
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables efficient and generalizable 3D reconstruction, but current feed-forward 3DGS methods for scene understanding remain largely category-oriented. In contrast, instance-aware 3DGS methods typically rely on per-scene optimization and often decouple reconstruction from instance and semantic learning, limiting reciprocal interactions among them. We present InstanceSplat, a unified feed-forward 3DGS framework for generalizable 3D reconstruction and instance-aware scene understanding from pose-free multi-view images. In a single forward pass, InstanceSplat constructs an instance-aware Gaussian representation that jointly encodes appearance, geometry, instance identity, and language-aligned semantics. Shared 3D Gaussians ground instance identities across views, producing renderable and cross-view-consistent instance features. To allow reconstruction and scene understanding to benefit from each other, we further design an instance-centric learning strategy that connects reconstruction, instance learning, and semantic learning through shared instance structure. Specifically, instance cues guide reconstruction, language-aligned semantics strengthen the discrimination of confusing same-category instances, and instance regions aggregate semantic evidence into coherent object-level predictions. Experiments on novel-view synthesis, instance segmentation, and open-vocabulary semantic understanding under varying input-view settings and on an unseen dataset demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, practical efficiency, and strong generalization.

AI.tldr: InstanceSplat is a unified feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that jointly performs generalizable 3D reconstruction and instance-aware scene understanding from pose-free multi-view images in a single forward pass, producing instance-aware Gaussian representations that encode appearance, geometry, instance identity, and language-aligned semantics with state-of-the-art performance across novel-view synthesis, instance segmentation, and open-vocabulary semantic understanding.
AI.motivation: Current feed-forward 3DGS methods for scene understanding are largely category-oriented, while instance-aware 3DGS methods typically rely on per-scene optimization and decouple reconstruction from instance and semantic learning, limiting reciprocal interactions among these tasks.
AI.method: InstanceSplat constructs an instance-aware Gaussian representation jointly encoding appearance, geometry, instance identity, and language-aligned semantics in a single forward pass. It uses shared 3D Gaussians to ground instance identities across views, producing renderable and cross-view-consistent instance features. An instance-centric learning strategy connects reconstruction, instance learning, and semantic learning through shared instance structure—instance cues guide reconstruction, language-aligned semantics discriminate confusing same-category instances, and instance regions aggregate semantic evidence into object-level predictions.
AI.result: Experiments show state-of-the-art performance on novel-view synthesis, instance segmentation, and open-vocabulary semantic understanding across varying input-view settings and on an unseen dataset, with practical efficiency and strong generalization.
AI.conclusion: InstanceSplat demonstrates that a unified feed-forward framework enabling reciprocal interactions between reconstruction and instance-aware scene understanding achieves superior performance and generalization compared to existing approaches.
